script.opening: "I’ve cracked a bone in my back just from a little stumble — the X-ray showed a fracture in my spine. I’ve been on steroid tablets for my polymyalgia for a couple of years. My daughter said steroids weaken bones — is that why this happened? Should I have been protected?"

facts.text: Stumbled on the rug at home 3 weeks ago and sat down hard; sudden mid-back pain. X-ray last week: "a crush fracture in the middle of my back". Pain sore getting out of a chair, "managing" with paracetamol. No leg weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel problems.

Prednisolone for polymyalgia for 2 years; started on 15 mg, "gone up and down", currently 7.5 mg. "I’d have to check the box." Has tried to come down below 5 mg twice and her shoulders "seized up". Never given a steroid card.
"No, never. That’s what’s bothering me." Never had a bone scan. Not on calcium or vitamin D. No one mentioned it.

Menopause at 47. Mother broke her hip at 75. No previous fractures. No kidney problems. Teeth: has a loose molar and is seeing the dentist next month. Heartburn occasionally. No weight loss, no bone pain elsewhere, no night sweats, not unusually tired.
BMI 22. Ex-smoker (stopped 20 years ago). 1–2 glasses of wine a week. Walks to the shops. One other fall last year in the garden.
Widowed; lives alone in a house with stairs. Daughter, Sue, a nurse, lives nearby.

Calm, direct, a little hurt. You want an honest answer. Respond warmly if the doctor is straightforward and apologetic where appropriate: "Thank you for being straight with me." If the doctor is defensive, become cooler. Ask how to take the bone tablet and whether you should stop going out.

ice.ideas: "My daughter says the steroids weakened my bones."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "That it’ll happen again, and that I should have been told." She is also afraid of having to stop the steroids, because her shoulders were "awful" before.
ice.expectations: "An honest answer, and to be put right."

cues: "Should I have been protected?" — honest, candour-style answer.
"I don’t want to give up the steroids" — the steroid must not be stopped abruptly; plan a review.
"I see the dentist next month" (if asked) — dental check before a bisphosphonate.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a low-trauma FRAGILITY FRACTURE as diagnostic of OSTEOPOROSIS and a marker of high future fracture risk

Recognises GLUCOCORTICOID-INDUCED OSTEOPOROSIS — that long-term/high-dose steroids markedly raise fracture risk (often before DEXA changes) — and that bone protection should have been started alongside the steroid (NOGG 7.5 mg for 3 months or more threshold), checking her current dose

Assesses fracture risk (FRAX ± DEXA) and STARTS bone protection now — a BISPHOSPHONATE with calcium/vitamin D — without waiting for DXA given the fragility fracture/steroid, after checking calcium, vitamin D, renal function and dental health, counselling administration/cautions

Reviews the GLUCOCORTICOID (lowest effective dose, planned taper, steroid-sparing agents/rheumatology review) to reduce ongoing harm, warning never to stop it abruptly and issuing a steroid emergency card

Addresses FALLS risk, lifestyle (weight-bearing exercise, smoking, alcohol, calcium/vitamin D) and fracture care, and checks other vertebral-fracture causes (myeloma screen per NICE NG12 1.10.4; metastasis if red flags), with a cord-compression safety-net
Communicates HONESTLY and openly (candour-style) that steroids contributed and protection is needed, without blame, apologising appropriately if protection was missed, and checks understanding
Explores her worry about further fractures and her confidence about staying on the steroid, and shares the decision about starting bone protection and adjusting the dose

Safety-nets and follows up: bone protection started and monitored, steroid review/taper, falls/lifestyle, fracture care, future bone monitoring, and honest follow-up — instituting protection and reviewing the steroid, not just treating the fracture

worked.txt: "Your daughter’s right to flag it, and I’ll be straight with you: long-term steroids do weaken bones, and they’re very likely a major reason this fracture happened. A fracture from a small stumble like this is itself a sign of osteoporosis."

"You ask a fair question — ideally, bone-protecting treatment is started alongside long-term steroids. If that wasn’t put in place, I’m sorry, and the important thing now is to put it right straight away."

"So I’m going to start you on a bone-strengthening tablet — a bisphosphonate like alendronate — with calcium and vitamin D. Given the fracture and the steroids, we don’t need to wait for a bone-density scan to begin. I’ll check your calcium, vitamin D and kidneys first, and please see your dentist for a check-up. I’ll explain how to take it (first thing, with a full glass of plain water, staying upright, before food)."

"We’ll also review your steroids — getting you onto the lowest dose that controls your polymyalgia, and considering with the rheumatology team whether a steroid-sparing medicine could reduce how much you need. Less steroid means kinder bones — but please don’t stop them suddenly, as your body relies on them now, and I’ll give you a steroid emergency card."
"Let’s also look at preventing falls, and weight-bearing exercise, stopping smoking and easing alcohol all help your bones, alongside managing the back pain."

"I’ll arrange follow-up, a bone scan as a baseline, and blood tests including a screen for other causes of a spinal fracture. Call 999 or go to A&E if you get new leg weakness or numbness, or problems with your bladder or bowels. Come back sooner if the pain is severe or you develop new symptoms like weight loss — occasionally spine fractures need further investigation."

f.learning: A LOW-TRAUMA (fragility) fracture — from standing height or less — is itself diagnostic of OSTEOPOROSIS and a strong marker of high future fracture risk, and a vertebral fragility fracture is significant. Long-term/high-dose oral GLUCOCORTICOIDS markedly increase fracture risk rapidly (often before DEXA changes), causing GLUCOCORTICOID-INDUCED OSTEOPOROSIS — so bone protection should ideally have been started with the steroid (NOGG: prednisolone 7.5 mg or more daily for 3 months or more), and steroids are very likely a major contributor here, which should be acknowledged honestly. Assess fracture risk (FRAX ± DEXA), but in a patient on long-term steroids with a fragility fracture START bone protection now — a BISPHOSPHONATE (e.g. alendronate) with calcium/vitamin D — without waiting for DXA, because a fragility fracture on long-term steroids is itself a treatment indication; check calcium, vitamin D, renal function and dental health first; counsel bisphosphonate administration (upright, with water, before food, oesophageal cautions) and monitoring. Review the glucocorticoid (lowest effective dose, planned taper where possible, steroid-sparing agents/rheumatology review) to reduce ongoing bone and other harm — never stopping it abruptly, and issuing a steroid emergency card (NatPSA/2020/005). Address falls risk (assessment/prevention), lifestyle (weight-bearing exercise, smoking, alcohol, adequate calcium/vitamin D) and fracture care (analgesia, mobilisation, physiotherapy), and check for other causes of vertebral fracture — NICE NG12 1.10.4 myeloma tests at 60 and over with unexplained fracture or back pain (FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains), metastasis if red flags — with a cord-compression safety-net. Communicate honestly and openly (a candour-style, non-defensive acknowledgement that steroids contributed and bone protection is now needed) without blame, apologising appropriately if protection was missed, and focus on putting it right with future bone monitoring. NICE NG12 myeloma testing (1.10.4) applies at her age with an unexplained fracture.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NOGG clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis (2021, updated 2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE NG259 (July 2026; replaced CG146) Osteoporosis: risk assessment · [4] NICE NG249 (2025) Falls: assessment and prevention · [5] NatPSA/2020/005/NHSPS (August 2020) steroid emergency card · [6] EULAR/ACR 2015 polymyalgia rheumatica recommendations (international) · [7] GMC and NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour (2015, updated 2022)
knowledge.summary: A vertebral fracture from a minor stumble in a 68-year-old on long-term prednisolone is a fragility fracture and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis until proved otherwise. Say honestly that the steroid very likely contributed. Start an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D now without waiting for a DXA scan, check bloods including a myeloma screen, review the steroid dose, assess falls and treat the pain.

points.t: A fracture from standing height or less is a fragility fracture. Vertebral fractures in particular predict further vertebral and hip fractures, so treat her as high risk [1]. Many vertebral fractures are painless and found by chance, so ask about height loss too.

Glucocorticoids raise fracture risk quickly, within months, and at bone density levels that would otherwise look safe [1]. NOGG: in postmenopausal women and men 50 and over starting 7.5 mg or more of prednisolone daily for 3 months or more, consider bone protection, started at the same time as the steroid and without waiting for DXA [1].

First-line: alendronate or risedronate (or IV zoledronate if oral is unsuitable), with calcium and vitamin D if intake is low [1]. Before starting, check calcium, vitamin D, renal function and dental health. Take the tablet on waking with a full glass of plain water, stay upright, and wait before food or other medicines, as the BNF describes. DXA can help baseline and monitoring but must not delay treatment [1].

NICE NG12: at 60 and over with persistent bone pain, especially back pain, or unexplained fracture, offer FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains [2]. NOGG also recommends bloods for secondary causes after a vertebral fracture [1].

points.h: Review the steroid, never stop it suddenly
points.t: Aim for the lowest dose that controls her polymyalgia. Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing option for people at risk of steroid harm [6], usually agreed with rheumatology. Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal glands: never stop abruptly, and give a steroid emergency card [5].

Assess falls using NICE NG249 triggers [4]. Treat the vertebral fracture pain with regular analgesia and keep her moving; physiotherapy helps. Weight-bearing exercise, not smoking, and alcohol within limits support bone health [1].

If bone protection should have been started with the steroid, say so plainly, apologise, explain what happens next and record the conversation [7]. Consider a significant event review in the practice.

Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis versus myeloma, metastasis and other secondary causes.
Screens cord or cauda equina symptoms, weight loss, night pain and falls.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

model.text: Hello, Mrs Hart, I’m Dr Shah. How can I help today?

I’ve cracked a bone in my back just from a little stumble. The X-ray showed a fracture in my spine. I’ve been on steroid tablets for my polymyalgia for a couple of years. My daughter said steroids weaken bones. Is that why this happened? Should I have been protected?
Those are really important questions and I’ll answer them honestly. First, how are you in yourself, and how is the pain?
model.why: Acknowledges both questions; checks wellbeing first

model.text: It’s sore, especially getting out of a chair. But I’m managing.
Can you tell me exactly how the fall happened? Did you fall from standing, or from a height?
Just a stumble at home, from standing. I didn’t even fall hard.
What dose of prednisolone are you on at the moment, and has it ever been stopped?
I’d have to check the box. It’s gone up and down, but I’ve been on it the whole two years.
That’s fine, I can check your record. Have you had any other falls, dizziness, or trouble with balance?
Not that I can think of. This was the first one.
Any numbness, weakness in your legs, or trouble passing water or opening your bowels since the fracture?
model.why: Screens cord or cauda equina compromise

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Have you lost weight without trying, had night sweats, or pain that wakes you at night?
No. Just the back pain when I move.
Has anyone ever talked to you about bone protection, or a bone density scan?
No, never. That’s what’s bothering me.
What worries you most about all this?
That it’ll happen again. And that I should have been told. I don’t want to give up the steroids either; my shoulders were awful before.
Those are fair worries. What would you like to come out of today?
An honest answer, and to be put right.

Your daughter is right. Long-term steroids weaken bones, and they are very likely a major reason a small stumble broke a bone in your spine. A fracture like this also tells us your bones are thin, which we call osteoporosis.
model.why: Links fragility fracture to glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis

model.text: So I should have been on something?

Yes. Guidance is that bone protection is usually started at the same time as long-term steroids, and I can’t see that it was offered to you. I’m sorry that didn’t happen. I’ll look into how it was missed, and my priority now is to put it right today.
Thank you for being straight with me.
I’d like to start a bone-strengthening tablet called alendronate, once a week, with calcium and vitamin D. We don’t need to wait for a scan. Does that sound all right?
model.why: Starts bisphosphonate without waiting for DXA

model.text: Yes. Is there a trick to taking it?

There is. Take it first thing on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, stay sitting or standing, and wait before breakfast or other tablets, as the leaflet says. Tell me about any heartburn or trouble swallowing. See your dentist for a check-up, and keep your teeth and gums healthy.
Okay. What about the steroids?

Please don’t stop them suddenly; your body relies on them now. I’ll give you a steroid emergency card. I’d like to ask the rheumatology team whether we can lower the dose or add a steroid-sparing medicine, so your shoulders stay comfortable with less steroid.
model.why: Steroid review; never stop abruptly; emergency card

model.text: That would be good.

I’ll also do some blood tests: your calcium, vitamin D and kidneys before the tablet, and a screen for other causes of a spinal fracture. I’ll arrange a bone density scan to give us a baseline. And for the pain, regular painkillers, keep gently moving, and physiotherapy.
model.why: Pre-treatment bloods, myeloma screen, DXA baseline, analgesia

model.text: Should I stop going out, in case I fall?
No, staying active protects your bones and balance. We’ll look at falls risks at home, and a physiotherapist can help with strength and balance.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you get new leg weakness or numbness, or problems with your bladder or bowels. Come back sooner if the pain gets much worse, you lose weight, or you feel unwell. I’ll see you in two weeks with the blood results.
model.why: Cord compromise, atypical features, planned review

model.text: Right.
Could you tell me the plan in your own words?

Weekly bone tablet with water, upright, before breakfast. Calcium and vitamin D. Don’t stop the steroids, carry the card, bloods and a scan, and you’ll ask the specialists about lowering the steroids.
Exactly right. Thank you for asking me so directly. It helps us put things right.

social.t: A spinal fracture can cause fear of going out. Encourage safe activity and offer strength and balance support so she does not become housebound.
Her daughter raised the question. With her consent, involving family can help with falls checks at home and medicine routines.

legal.t: GMC and NMC professional duty of candour (2015, updated 2022): tell the patient when something has gone wrong, apologise, explain, and offer to put it right. Record the discussion. She may complain; tell her how the practice complaints process works if she asks.

professional.t: A missed bone-protection opportunity is a learning event. Review the practice’s steroid prescribing so other patients on long-term steroids are checked for bone protection.
Steroid-sparing drugs such as methotrexate need specialist advice and monitoring. Agree who prescribes and monitors.

community.t: The Royal Osteoporosis Society has information and a helpline. Many areas have a fracture liaison service and community falls services.

redFlags: New leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change (cord or cauda equina compromise)
Weight loss, night pain, feeling unwell (myeloma or metastasis; NICE NG12 1.10.4 tests at 60 and over)
psychosocial: Feeling let down that protection was not offered
Dependence on the steroid for her symptoms
ice: Idea: the steroids weakened her bones
Concern: another fracture, and that something was missed
Expectation: an honest answer and to be put right

playbook.diagnosis: “This is a fragility fracture of the spine caused by osteoporosis, and the long-term steroids are very likely a major cause.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Bone is always being broken down and rebuilt, like a wall being repaired brick by brick. Steroids slow the builders down, so the wall gets thinner. The bone tablet slows the demolition crew, so the wall can strengthen again.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked whether the steroids caused this and whether you should have been protected. The honest answer to both is yes, and I’m sorry. Let’s put it right today.”
management.psychosocial: Apologise clearly without blaming colleagues; keep her active and confident; involve her daughter if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate, dose per BNF) with calcium and vitamin D, started now (NOGG)
Before starting: calcium, vitamin D, renal function; dental check
Bloods for secondary causes, including myeloma screen (NICE NG12 1.10.4); baseline DXA
Do not stop prednisolone suddenly; steroid emergency card (NatPSA 2020); rheumatology advice on dose reduction or steroid-sparing drug
Analgesia, physiotherapy and falls assessment (NICE NG249)
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change
Return for worsening pain, weight loss or feeling unwell; review in 2 weeks with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by treating only the fracture, by dodging the honesty question, and by unsafe steroid advice. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Managing the pain and sending her home.
items.why: A low-trauma vertebral fracture signals osteoporosis and high future fracture risk (NOGG).
items.fix: Name it a fragility fracture and start bone protection today.

items.fail: Waiting for a DXA scan before treating.
items.why: NOGG advises starting bone protection without waiting for DXA in people on long-term steroids at high risk.
items.fix: Start a bisphosphonate now; use DXA as a baseline.

items.why: NICE NG12 1.10.4 recommends myeloma tests at 60 and over with unexplained fracture or back pain.
items.fix: Screen for red flags and send FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, electrophoresis and free light chains.

items.fail: Telling her to stop or cut the steroid herself.
items.why: Adrenal suppression makes sudden withdrawal dangerous.
items.fix: Keep the dose, issue a steroid emergency card, and plan a supervised reduction with rheumatology.

items.fail: Defensive or vague answers about the missed protection.
items.why: She asked directly; evasion damages trust and falls short of the duty of candour.
items.fix: Say what should have happened, apologise, and explain the plan to put it right.

items.fail: No bisphosphonate counselling or dental advice.
items.why: Wrong administration causes oesophageal harm and poor absorption; dental health matters with bisphosphonates (BNF).
items.fix: Explain how to take it, ask about heartburn, advise a dental check; teach-back.

timeMap.d: Hear both questions; promise an honest answer; check pain.
Mechanism, steroid dose and duration, falls, neurological symptoms, weight loss and night pain, previous bone protection.
Fear of another fracture, feeling let down, wants to keep the steroid.
Fragility fracture from steroid-induced osteoporosis; clear apology that protection was not started.
Bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D, counselling, bloods and myeloma screen, DXA, steroid review and card, falls, safety-net, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats the fracture as a simple injury with painkillers; avoids answering whether protection was missed; waits for a DXA before any treatment; tells her to cut down the steroid herself.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the fragility fracture and steroid link, answers honestly, starts a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D, and plans a steroid review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: apologises clearly and records it; counsels bisphosphonate use and dental care; checks calcium, vitamin D and renal function and screens for myeloma; steroid emergency card and warning not to stop suddenly; falls assessment; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s hard to say what caused it; lots of things weaken bones.”
avoid.instead: “The steroids are very likely a major reason this happened.”
avoid.why: Evasive answers break trust and fall short of the professional duty of candour.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get a bone scan first and then decide about treatment.”
avoid.instead: “With this fracture and your steroids, we can start treatment today.”
avoid.why: NOGG: start bone protection without waiting for DXA in this group.

avoid.instead: “Don’t stop them suddenly; I’ll ask the specialists how to lower them safely.”
avoid.why: Abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis and a flare of polymyalgia.

SCA_STEM.recent: Spinal X-ray after a minor stumble shows a vertebral fracture. No bone protection recorded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Wants to know if her steroid tablets caused the spinal fracture, and whether she should have been protected.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NOGG clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis (2021, updated 2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE NG259 (July 2026; replaced CG146) Osteoporosis: risk assessment · [4] NICE NG249 (2025) Falls: assessment and prevention · [5] NatPSA/2020/005/NHSPS (August 2020) steroid emergency card · [6] EULAR/ACR 2015 polymyalgia rheumatica recommendations (international) · [7] GMC and NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour (2015, updated 2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A vertebral fracture from a minor stumble in a 68-year-old on long-term prednisolone is a fragility fracture and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis until proved otherwise. Say honestly that the steroid very likely contributed. Start an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D now without waiting for a DXA scan, check bloods including a myeloma screen, review the steroid dose, assess falls and treat the pain.

points.t: A fracture from standing height or less is a fragility fracture. Vertebral fractures in particular predict further vertebral and hip fractures, so treat her as high risk [1]. Many vertebral fractures are painless and found by chance, so ask about height loss too.

Glucocorticoids raise fracture risk quickly, within months, and at bone density levels that would otherwise look safe [1]. NOGG: in postmenopausal women and men 50 and over starting 7.5 mg or more of prednisolone daily for 3 months or more, consider bone protection, started at the same time as the steroid and without waiting for DXA [1].

First-line: alendronate or risedronate (or IV zoledronate if oral is unsuitable), with calcium and vitamin D if intake is low [1]. Before starting, check calcium, vitamin D, renal function and dental health. Take the tablet on waking with a full glass of plain water, stay upright, and wait before food or other medicines, as the BNF describes. DXA can help baseline and monitoring but must not delay treatment [1].

NICE NG12: at 60 and over with persistent bone pain, especially back pain, or unexplained fracture, offer FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains [2]. NOGG also recommends bloods for secondary causes after a vertebral fracture [1].

points.h: Review the steroid, never stop it suddenly
points.t: Aim for the lowest dose that controls her polymyalgia. Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing option for people at risk of steroid harm [6], usually agreed with rheumatology. Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal glands: never stop abruptly, and give a steroid emergency card [5].

Assess falls using NICE NG249 triggers [4]. Treat the vertebral fracture pain with regular analgesia and keep her moving; physiotherapy helps. Weight-bearing exercise, not smoking, and alcohol within limits support bone health [1].

If bone protection should have been started with the steroid, say so plainly, apologise, explain what happens next and record the conversation [7]. Consider a significant event review in the practice.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets her ask both questions and checks pain and wellbeing first.
Fear of further fractures; reliance on the steroid for her shoulders; family involvement through her daughter.
Picks up “should I have been protected?” as a request for honesty; hears the wish to keep the steroid.
Idea (the steroids caused it), concern (recurrence and a missed opportunity), expectation (an honest answer and a fix).
Calcium, vitamin D, renal function; myeloma screen per NICE NG12 1.10.4; baseline DXA without delaying treatment; neurological screen.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis versus myeloma, metastasis and other secondary causes.
Screens cord or cauda equina symptoms, weight loss, night pain and falls.
Fragility vertebral fracture from glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.
Oral bisphosphonate now with calcium and vitamin D (NOGG); administration and dental advice; analgesia and physiotherapy.
Steroid review with rheumatology, steroid-sparing option; never stop abruptly; steroid emergency card; falls assessment.
999 for leg weakness or sphincter change; return for worse pain or weight loss; review with bloods in 2 weeks; candour recorded.

social.t: A spinal fracture can cause fear of going out. Encourage safe activity and offer strength and balance support so she does not become housebound.
Her daughter raised the question. With her consent, involving family can help with falls checks at home and medicine routines.

legal.t: GMC and NMC professional duty of candour (2015, updated 2022): tell the patient when something has gone wrong, apologise, explain, and offer to put it right. Record the discussion. She may complain; tell her how the practice complaints process works if she asks.

professional.t: A missed bone-protection opportunity is a learning event. Review the practice’s steroid prescribing so other patients on long-term steroids are checked for bone protection.
Steroid-sparing drugs such as methotrexate need specialist advice and monitoring. Agree who prescribes and monitors.

community.t: The Royal Osteoporosis Society has information and a helpline. Many areas have a fracture liaison service and community falls services.

redFlags: New leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change (cord or cauda equina compromise)
Weight loss, night pain, feeling unwell (myeloma or metastasis; NICE NG12 1.10.4 tests at 60 and over)
psychosocial: Feeling let down that protection was not offered
Dependence on the steroid for her symptoms
ice: Idea: the steroids weakened her bones
Concern: another fracture, and that something was missed
Expectation: an honest answer and to be put right

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is a fragility fracture of the spine caused by osteoporosis, and the long-term steroids are very likely a major cause.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Bone is always being broken down and rebuilt, like a wall being repaired brick by brick. Steroids slow the builders down, so the wall gets thinner. The bone tablet slows the demolition crew, so the wall can strengthen again.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked whether the steroids caused this and whether you should have been protected. The honest answer to both is yes, and I’m sorry. Let’s put it right today.”
management.psychosocial: Apologise clearly without blaming colleagues; keep her active and confident; involve her daughter if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate, dose per BNF) with calcium and vitamin D, started now (NOGG)
Before starting: calcium, vitamin D, renal function; dental check
Bloods for secondary causes, including myeloma screen (NICE NG12 1.10.4); baseline DXA
Do not stop prednisolone suddenly; steroid emergency card (NatPSA 2020); rheumatology advice on dose reduction or steroid-sparing drug
Analgesia, physiotherapy and falls assessment (NICE NG249)
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for leg weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change
Return for worsening pain, weight loss or feeling unwell; review in 2 weeks with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by treating only the fracture, by dodging the honesty question, and by unsafe steroid advice. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Managing the pain and sending her home.
items.why: A low-trauma vertebral fracture signals osteoporosis and high future fracture risk (NOGG).
items.fix: Name it a fragility fracture and start bone protection today.

items.fail: Waiting for a DXA scan before treating.
items.why: NOGG advises starting bone protection without waiting for DXA in people on long-term steroids at high risk.
items.fix: Start a bisphosphonate now; use DXA as a baseline.

items.why: NICE NG12 1.10.4 recommends myeloma tests at 60 and over with unexplained fracture or back pain.
items.fix: Screen for red flags and send FBC, calcium, ESR or plasma viscosity, electrophoresis and free light chains.

items.fail: Telling her to stop or cut the steroid herself.
items.why: Adrenal suppression makes sudden withdrawal dangerous.
items.fix: Keep the dose, issue a steroid emergency card, and plan a supervised reduction with rheumatology.

items.fail: Defensive or vague answers about the missed protection.
items.why: She asked directly; evasion damages trust and falls short of the duty of candour.
items.fix: Say what should have happened, apologise, and explain the plan to put it right.

items.fail: No bisphosphonate counselling or dental advice.
items.why: Wrong administration causes oesophageal harm and poor absorption; dental health matters with bisphosphonates (BNF).
items.fix: Explain how to take it, ask about heartburn, advise a dental check; teach-back.
